interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and three retained runs now answer it for VerifyLeader while showing that the same strand follows channel buffering rather than the API. In this run the VerifyLeader strand reproduced (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13, comparison 4 holds), and so did the contrast: with the default unbuffered applyCh, Barrier and Apply answered every one of their eight post-shutdown calls in all three trials (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17; comparisons 2 and 3 hold). The new batched cases, where BatchApplyCh buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries, show the flip: Barrier answered 4, 5 and 6 of eight post-shutdown calls (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply answered 4, 4 and 3 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 4, 3 and 2 and then 4, 4 and 5 futures unanswered after 500ms, in each case with the rest answered by 'raft is already shutdown'. The mechanism is therefore pinned by a configuration change: only the channel's buffering differs between the answered and the stranded cases, since Config.BatchApplyCh exists exactly to buffer applyCh and its own comment warns that it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply. The declared comparisons for those new cases came back unresolved rather than satisfied, because the batched cases reuse the same trial and kind as the unbuffered ones, so the setup event that admits each result event is ambiguous; the event values themselves are recorded and decisive, and a corrected revision that gives the batched cases distinct trial identifiers and records batch_apply_ch on the setup event as well is submitted with this update. What the three runs together establish is narrower and firmer than the first account: the racing phase is the fragile part (9 and 41 of 64 in the first run, 0 of 128 in the two later ones), while the post-shutdown phase is stable, and the defect is confined to call kinds whose channel is buffered, with VerifyLeader always in that set and the apply path only when BatchApplyCh is enabled.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the two later runs (0 of 128 per case), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.
Without BatchApplyCh, Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in any run (0 of 192, 0 of 384 and 0 of 384 attempts), so the defect does not touch the default apply path.

Every call that was answered returned success or the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, so no completed call carries a wrong outcome.
limitations: The batched counts come from three trials of eight post-shutdown calls each (Barrier 4, 5, 6 answered; Apply 4, 4, 3 answered) in one execution, so they bound the mechanism rather than a population rate.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source, since no reader of the affected channel remains and these futures have no shutdown channel.
Single-voter node with in-memory transport and 50ms timeouts; no peer round trip or networked shutdown is involved.

scope.description: Run the shutdown probe for VerifyLeader, Barrier and Apply with the default unbuffered applyCh and for Barrier and Apply with BatchApplyCh enabled, three trials each, recording racing and post-shutdown completion counts and the batch_apply_ch flag, with a no-shutdown control; the batched cases use distinct trial identifiers so each result event is admitted by a single setup event.
assumptions: BatchApplyCh is a supported option whose documented effect is to buffer applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and to break the timeout guarantee on Apply.
MaxAppendEntries (the default) is large enough that the post-shutdown sends never block, so the buffered send stays selectable exactly as verifyCh's does.
Single-voter node, in-memory transport, 50ms timeouts, one process.
excluded: Multi-node behaviour and buffer sizes small enough to block the sends.

experiment.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms and BatchApplyCh set only for the batched cases, and waits until it reports Leader. It emits assurance_shutdown_setup carrying trial, kind, shutdown, batch_apply_ch, the call counts and the window, then issues 128 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 4000ms deadline, and in the shutdown cases calls Shutdown() from a goroutine 2ms later. After Shutdown returns it issues 8 further calls one at a time with a 500ms wait each and emits assurance_shutdown_result with the racing counts, the post-phase counts and histograms, the shutdown error, the node state and batch_apply_ch. Batched barrier and apply cases use trial identifiers 100 to 102 so their setup and result events are distinguishable from the unbuffered ones. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: Barrier with BatchApplyCh: at least one post-shutdown call left unanswered, which would confirm the strand follows buffering.

Barrier with the default unbuffered applyCh: every post-shutdown call answered.
Apply with the default unbuffered applyCh: same contrast.
VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered: the strand re-measured alongside the batched cases.

Cases, event names and measured fields are otherwise unchanged.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous harness emitted CA_EVENT objects without an event name, so the controller rejected all three as invalid_observation and no observation could be interpreted. This revision only changes the observation format: each case now emits a named assurance_partition_setup event before the partition and a named assurance_verify_leader_result event afterwards, carrying the same measured fields, and declares the setup event as a prerequisite admission with one comparison per partition case.

scope.description: Observe what LeadershipTransferToServer reports against which server actually takes leadership when the requested target is a non-voter, with the same call naming a voter as the only difference. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event describing the leader, the chosen target, its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration and the voter set, then an assurance_transfer_result event with the returned result, the target's and old leader's states, the leader set and terms after the call, and the time until any leader is observed.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; protocol version is the default (>= 3), so LeadershipTransferToServer is supported.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a real transfer rather than a probe that never succeeds.
excluded: Bounding the length of any leaderless interval: leadership state is sampled at the end of the 1500ms observation window, so this probe does not measure an interval.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming them as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is then chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: in the control case the first voter that is not the leader, in the probe case the joined non-voter; its suffrage is read back from the leader's latest configuration and reported in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr), waits up to 5s for the returned result, then waits up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader and separately for any node to be Leader, and finally records the leader set, the maximum term across all four nodes and whether that term rose above the leader's term before the call. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget and are emitted under distinct case names.

scope.description: Observe both halves of a leadership transfer request naming a non-voter: what LeadershipTransferToServer reports, which server actually holds leadership, and how the cluster's leadership state evolves during the attempt, sampled every millisecond, with the same call naming a voter as the control. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event and an assurance_transfer_result event carrying the returned result, the target and previous-leader states, leader sets and terms, and the sampling counters.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate, and protocol version >= 3 supports LeadershipTransferToServer.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a completed transfer.

Sampling every millisecond is fine-grained relative to the 200ms election timeout, so a leaderless interval lasting an election round is expected to be visible; shorter gaps are not bounded by this sampling rate.
excluded: Process-level stalls, host suspends and multi-host clock behaviour, which a single-process in-memory probe does not reproduce.

experiments.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Run eight independent trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, arm a 600ms stall in the leader's log store, partition the leader so that only the non-voter remains reachable, drive a client Apply to block the leader's main loop on that store, queue VerifyLeader during the stall, and report the verify endpoint together with a 1ms leadership sampler over all four servers.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stalls; StoreLogs then blocks the leader's main loop, which is the goroutine that also serves the lease case and verify requests. The store is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; the stall is 600ms, three times the lease.
Only the elected leader's store is armed, so follower writes and their election timers behave as they would without the stall.
In-memory transports are used in one process, so RPC round trips are much faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: A leader blocked inside its own lease check rather than inside a store write, and host-level suspensions or clock jumps, which this probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store that wraps InmemStore and sleeps for 600ms inside StoreLogs while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's own AddNonvoter call, with the trial waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The trial then emits assurance_stall_setup, disconnects the transports in both directions across the partition so that only the leader and the non-voter remain mutually reachable, starts a 1ms sampler that records every server's Leader state and the maximum term, arms the leader's stall, drives one Apply to make the leader write, queues VerifyLeader 300ms later, and reports assurance_stall_trial with the verify endpoint, the sample counters, the term reached, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyLeaderDuringLeaderStall.

comparisons.description: The stall was exercised and a different server was observed in Leader state at some point during or after it. Holds means the intended condition was reached.
Conditional on a successor having been observed: whether the queued VerifyLeader still reported success. Holds means the stale-read precondition was witnessed.
Restricted to trials where the stalled leader was never sampled outside Leader state: whether VerifyLeader reported success.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.
excluded: Whether a stuck future can be recovered by any other API, and any multi-node variant where a future could still be answered by another goroutine after shutdown.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance in this process with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, and waits until it reports Leader. It then emits assurance_shutdown_setup and issues 64 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 1500ms local deadline and recording whether it returned and with which error. Concurrently, in the shutdown cases, Shutdown() is called and the case waits for it to return, then sleeps 400ms so that any future which can still be answered has been, and finally waits for all per-call timers before emitting assurance_shutdown_result with the returned and stuck counts, the outcome histogram, the shutdown error and the node state. The no-shutdown control issues the same calls without ever calling Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: VerifyLeader against a concurrent shutdown: at least one future never completed. Holds means the predicted hang was observed.
VerifyLeader control without shutdown: no future is left incomplete, so incompleteness is not a property of the probe itself.
Barrier against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears on the apply-channel path, which the harness drains in batches.

The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

Every future that did complete in these trials reported success, so the hang is confined to calls that were never served; no completed call was answered with a wrong outcome.
limitations: The probe deliberately uses 64 concurrent VerifyLeader calls to make queue occupancy likely; it does not measure the probability for a single call racing Shutdown, only that the race exists.
The single-voter configuration removes commit latency as a confounder but also means verify requests need no peer round trip, so nothing else can be holding the queue.

Whether a stuck future could ever be answered later is inferred from the source and from the node reporting Shutdown complete with no loop running; the harness waited 1500ms per call and 400ms after Shutdown returned, not indefinitely.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and both retained runs say yes for VerifyLeader while excluding the other two. The revision isolates the mechanism better than the first run did, because its post-shutdown phase has no race with the shutdown itself: in the three verify cases (parsed result events at indices 1, 7 and 13) only 4, 3 and 3 of the 8 calls made after Shutdown() had returned were answered, all with 'raft is already shutdown', while the other 4, 5 and 5 returned futures that were still incomplete 500ms later and can never be answered because the run loop, the FSM goroutine and every other reader of verifyCh have already exited. That is 14 of 24 post-shutdown VerifyLeader calls stranded, and it is a per-call coin flip rather than a rare race. The same receipt shows the contrast in the two other call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all 48 of their post-shutdown calls with the shutdown error (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17), and no call in the racing phase of any case was left incomplete (0 stuck out of 128 per case, with 128 answered in the no-shutdown control at index 19). The source explains exactly that split. VerifyLeader builds a verifyFuture whose init() allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), so nothing sets ShutdownCh and deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117); the call then selects between the closed shutdown channel and a send into verifyCh, which is buffered with 64 slots (api.go 576), so the send is ready with no receiver and the select returns an unanswerable future whenever it picks that case. Barrier and ApplyLog use the same select shape (api.go 907-926 and 874-899) but send to applyCh, which is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh is set (api.go 549), so once the loop has exited their send cannot be selected and the shutdown case always wins. The repository's own test file already notes the class as a TODO for Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration (raft_test.go 38-42), which is an admission of the gap rather than a contract that permits it. The first receipt adds the racing form of the same defect: with 64 calls issued just before Shutdown and a 1500ms wait, two of its three verify trials left 9 and 41 futures incomplete while the control left none (indices 1, 7, 13 and 19 there). The revision's racing phase left none, so that form is timing dependent; the post-shutdown form is not, and it is the one the account now rests on.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the revision: 0 of 128 calls per case were left incomplete, so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in either run (0 of 192 and 0 of 192 in the first receipt; 0 of 384 in the revision), which limits the defect to the VerifyLeader path unless BatchApplyCh is enabled.
Every call that was answered in these runs returned success or the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, so the defect is confined to calls whose future is never served.

The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence that the gap was noticed; it does not make the documented ErrRaftShutdown behaviour any less expected for a caller.
limitations: The post-shutdown counts come from 24 VerifyLeader calls in one execution (14 stranded); they bound the mechanism, not a population rate, and the per-call split is consistent with an unbiased select rather than a measured probability.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source (no reader of verifyCh remains and ShutdownCh is nil on these futures) rather than observed indefinitely.
A single-voter node with in-memory transport and 50ms timeouts is used, so no peer round trip or networked shutdown is involved.
A BatchApplyCh configuration, where applyCh becomes buffered and the apply path should inherit the same defect, has not been measured.
interpretations.joint_history: Both receipts come from the same harness lineage: receipt a1933fdba3e74bd1b98cd6e8dcd138c4 is the fixed experiment b2ccc787c9384b008b5f9c668746f760-experiment and receipt b3b821a061f346a1aa27e3fee5e44cb9 is its revision 49fa455b2fe94d53ab6fed2fad19ce33-experiment, which kept the event names, the case kinds and every measured field and changed only the completion window (1500ms to 4000ms), the call count (64 to 128), an interleaved 2ms shutdown and the added post-shutdown phase. result.summary: Interpreted the BatchApplyCh receipt and requested the correction it needs. VerifyLeader's strand reproduced (indices 1, 7, 13) and so did the unbuffered contrast: Barrier and Apply answered all eight post-shutdown calls in every trial (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17). The new batched cases show the flip — with applyCh buffered, Barrier answered 4, 5 and 6 of eight post-shutdown calls and Apply 4, 4 and 3, leaving the rest unanswered after 500ms — which pins the mechanism to channel buffering, since Config.BatchApplyCh exists precisely to buffer applyCh and its own comment warns it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply. The declared comparisons for those cases came back unresolved rather than satisfied because the batched cases reuse trial and kind with the unbuffered ones, making the admitting setup event ambiguous; I recorded the event-level values, noted that limitation explicitly, and submitted a revision that gives the batched cases trial identifiers 100-102 and carries batch_apply_ch on the setup event too. Joint history across the three harness revisions is recorded, and no earlier receipt is withdrawn.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Run eight independent trials that each build a three-voter plus one-non-voter cluster, arm a 600ms stall in the leader's log store, partition the leader so that only the non-voter remains reachable, drive a client Apply to block the leader's main loop on that store, queue VerifyLeader during the stall, and report the verify endpoint together with a 1ms leadership sampler over all four servers.
assumptions: The stalling log store models a leader whose disk stalls; StoreLogs then blocks the leader's main loop, which is the goroutine that also serves the lease case and verify requests. The store is a supplied dependency, not a change to production logic.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate; the stall is 600ms, three times the lease.
Only the elected leader's store is armed, so follower writes and their election timers behave as they would without the stall.
In-memory transports are used in one process, so RPC round trips are much faster than in a networked cluster.
excluded: A leader blocked inside its own lease check rather than inside a store write, and host-level suspensions or clock jumps, which this probe does not reproduce.

basis.prefix: Each trial builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts; the three voters get a log store that wraps InmemStore and sleeps for 600ms inside StoreLogs while armed, and only the elected leader's store is armed. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter and the fourth node joins through the leader's own AddNonvoter call, with the trial waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The trial then emits assurance_stall_setup, disconnects the transports in both directions across the partition so that only the leader and the non-voter remain mutually reachable, starts a 1ms sampler that records every server's Leader state and the maximum term, arms the leader's stall, drives one Apply to make the leader write, queues VerifyLeader 300ms later, and reports assurance_stall_trial with the verify endpoint, the sample counters, the term reached, and the stall counters. The harness is TestAssuranceVerifyLeaderDuringLeaderStall.

comparisons.description: The stall was exercised and a different server was observed in Leader state at some point during or after it. Holds means the intended condition was reached.
Conditional on a successor having been observed: whether the queued VerifyLeader still reported success. Holds means the stale-read precondition was witnessed.
Restricted to trials where the stalled leader was never sampled outside Leader state: whether VerifyLeader reported success.

scope.description: Issue 64 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls in parallel against a freshly started single-voter node while Shutdown runs concurrently, count how many of those futures have not completed 400ms after Shutdown has returned, and compare with the same call kinds issued on a node that is never shut down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histogram and the shutdown error.
assumptions: A single-voter node is a supported configuration and makes each call complete quickly when the node is running, so any incomplete future is attributable to the shutdown race rather than to slow commit.
64 concurrent calls per trial is a probe of exposure, not a rate estimate; the concurrency is what makes the race observable.
Waiting 400ms after Shutdown() has returned is enough for any future that can still be answered, because the run loop has already exited by then.
excluded: Whether a stuck future can be recovered by any other API, and any multi-node variant where a future could still be answered by another goroutine after shutdown.

basis.prefix: Each case starts one real Raft instance in this process with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, bootstrapped as a single Voter with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, and waits until it reports Leader. It then emits assurance_shutdown_setup and issues 64 calls of the chosen kind from separate goroutines, each waiting on Error() with a 1500ms local deadline and recording whether it returned and with which error. Concurrently, in the shutdown cases, Shutdown() is called and the case waits for it to return, then sleeps 400ms so that any future which can still be answered has been, and finally waits for all per-call timers before emitting assurance_shutdown_result with the returned and stuck counts, the outcome histogram, the shutdown error and the node state. The no-shutdown control issues the same calls without ever calling Shutdown. The harness is TestAssuranceShutdownFutureCompletion.

comparisons.description: VerifyLeader against a concurrent shutdown: at least one future never completed. Holds means the predicted hang was observed.
VerifyLeader control without shutdown: no future is left incomplete, so incompleteness is not a property of the probe itself.
Barrier against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears on the apply-channel path, which the harness drains in batches.
Apply against a concurrent shutdown: whether the same hang appears for command application.

scope.description: In three trials per call kind, issue 128 VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply calls while Shutdown is interleaved into the fill, count how many of those futures are still incomplete 4000ms later, then issue 8 further calls of the same kind after Shutdown has returned and record whether each is answered within 500ms; a no-shutdown control runs the same call kinds without ever shutting down. Each case emits an assurance_shutdown_setup event and an assurance_shutdown_result event carrying the counts, the outcome histograms for both phases and the shutdown error.
assumptions: VerifyLeader is a legal call at any time, including after Shutdown, and the documented generic error for that case is ErrRaftShutdown, which the API's own select returns when the shutdown channel is chosen.
A single-voter node removes commit latency as a confounder and makes every call complete in well under a millisecond while the node is running.
The 4000ms window is long enough that a future answered only by the exited run loop would show as incomplete; nothing else in the harness can answer these futures.
excluded: A BatchApplyCh configuration, where applyCh becomes buffered and the apply path should behave like the verify path; and multi-node variants.

scope.description: Run the shutdown probe for VerifyLeader, Barrier and Apply with the default unbuffered applyCh and again for Barrier and Apply with BatchApplyCh enabled, three trials each, recording how many futures are left incomplete in the racing phase and how many of eight post-shutdown calls are answered in the 500ms window, plus a no-shutdown control.
assumptions: BatchApplyCh is a supported configuration option whose documented effect is to buffer applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and to break the timeout guarantee on Apply.
Buffer size is MaxAppendEntries (the default), which is large enough that the eight post-shutdown sends never block, so the send case is selectable exactly as verifyCh's is.
Single-voter node, in-memory transport, 50ms timeouts, one process, as before.
excluded: BatchApplyCh with BatchApplyChMaxAppendEntries or concurrency large enough to fill the buffer, and multi-node behaviour.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. The consequence for reads is bounded rather than unconditional: checkLeaderLease uses voters only, so under a validated configuration the lease normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and the acknowledgements counted while the leader is still legitimately leader are not themselves stale. The account therefore asserts a defect in the decision support VerifyLeader provides (success without voter-majority acknowledgement) and treats the stale-read consequence as conditional on the lease's timing assumption (a leader stall, clock jump or lease check interleaving that lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports success). The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the result: the partition, not the outcome, selects the peer, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path.
counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; this bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing VerifyLeader's decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a follower's election timer normally fires no earlier than the lease that causes the old leader to step down; the new-leader half of a stale read is therefore usually prevented by the lease rather than by the verify quorum.

interpretations.rationale: The documented purpose of LeadershipTransferToServer is to transition leadership to a specific server in the cluster, and the only target validation in the leader is a lookup in leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader regardless of Suffrage; a missing entry is the sole error. A non-voter therefore passes validation and is sent TimeoutNow, which makes it a Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote so the node sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Voters processing that request adopt the higher term and set themselves to Follower before the hasVote check rejects the candidate, so the candidate cannot collect a single grant, while the old leader loses leadership because it adopts the higher term too and its transfer goroutine then reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch. The account is asserted on that source basis and stays conditional until the requested two-case probe reports what the call returns versus which server actually takes leadership; the controlling contrast is the same call naming a voter, and the note that auto-targeted LeadershipTransfer() skips non-voters via pickServer shows the library itself does not consider a non-voter a valid transfer target when it chooses.
counterevidence: The API does not state in its comment that the target must be a voter, and a caller who names only voters never reaches this path, so the defect depends on an accepted calling pattern rather than on the library's own choice of target.

LeadershipTransfer() without an explicit target filters non-voters in pickServer, which shows the intended transfer target set is the voter set and supports reading the targeted call as requiring the same premise.
A TimeoutNow that cannot be delivered (unreachable target) is reported as an error by the transfer path, so not every unusable target is silently accepted.
limitations: No receipt exists yet for this question; the harness for the two-case probe is submitted with this update and its outcome is predicted, not observed.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.

The remaining trigger was a leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease; the child question's probe exercised exactly that in eight trials and reached the condition (a successor at term 3 while the stalled leader stayed Leader, first seen at 345-464ms) without producing a verify success, because the lease case was already ready when the loop resumed and leadership was given up before the non-voter's acknowledgement could be counted. What is left is the sub-millisecond interleaving in which that acknowledgement is counted in the same iteration in which the loop resumes, which these trials neither reached nor bounded.

The grant side bounds the consequence more tightly than the verify quorum does: because a voter refuses votes while it knows another leader, no successor can be elected before HeartbeatTimeout plus an election round after the last leader contact, while the lease removes the old leader at LeaderLeaseTimeout + minCheckInterval at the latest; with the documented defaults the two cannot overlap, and even when LeaderLeaseTimeout equals HeartbeatTimeout the residual is a few milliseconds.

A targeted attempt at the stall trigger failed to produce the consequence: eight trials with a leader blocked in StoreLogs past its lease, a successor elected at term 3, and only a non-voter reachable all answered the queued verify with leadership loss or not-the-leader rather than success (receipt 2e5f37f634834b8197227626ed6d99b7, result indices 1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15).
limitations: Repeatability under the same fixed input is now shown for one additional run: receipt 107a6d6c816d448da2b7ff6e3145bac1 reproduces all three outcomes of receipt b02d5ff23a504a8ea38116085ba8e23c, with the non-voter-only partition returning success in 0ms while the leader stayed Leader, the voter-only control also returning success, and the no-peer partition returning 'leadership lost while committing log' at 208ms against 202ms in the first run. The two step-down times are the schedule-dependent quantity in that control; a repeat under the same timeouts and transports shows reproducibility, not schedule independence or independence from the JIT of the harness.

The stale-read consequence needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, and the two orderings that decide it are both in the source. A voter refuses a vote or a pre-vote while it still knows a leader other than the candidate (raft.go 1673-1679 and 1786-1792), and it clears that knowledge only in its own campaign path, which runs after HeartbeatTimeout without leader contact (raft.go 227-228). A successor therefore needs a quorum of voters that have already reached that trigger, so it cannot exist earlier than HeartbeatTimeout after their last contact with the old leader, plus the election rounds. The leader, meanwhile, steps down at the first lease check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout, and ValidateConfig allows LeaderLeaseTimeout to equal HeartbeatTimeout: in the worst schedule the boundary check still counts the voter (the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout) and the step-down follows after minCheckInterval = 10ms. So under a validated configuration the leader leaves office in at most LeaderLeaseTimeout + 10ms, which is at most HeartbeatTimeout + 10ms, while no successor can be elected before HeartbeatTimeout plus a round of pre-vote and vote. The residual exposure is therefore confined to configurations with LeaderLeaseTimeout == HeartbeatTimeout and schedules where the granters clear at the earliest instant, and it is a few milliseconds at most; the practical route to a longer exposure is a leader whose own goroutine is stalled or whose clock jumps, which the earlier account relied on.

The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks; the partition was made by disconnecting transports in both directions.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO for Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration, which is a source admission that the gap exists rather than a contract that permits it; it is cited here as evidence about intent, not as a reason to withhold the finding.
Every future that did complete in these trials reported success, so the hang is confined to calls that were never served; no completed call was answered with a wrong outcome.
limitations: The probe deliberately uses 64 concurrent VerifyLeader calls to make queue occupancy likely; it does not measure the probability for a single call racing Shutdown, only that the race exists.
The single-voter configuration removes commit latency as a confounder but also means verify requests need no peer round trip, so nothing else can be holding the queue.

Whether a stuck future could ever be answered later is inferred from the source and from the node reporting Shutdown complete with no loop running; the harness waited 1500ms per call and 400ms after Shutdown returned, not indefinitely.
The counts varied widely across trials (9, 41, 0), so the true rate is not bounded by this execution.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and both retained runs say yes for VerifyLeader while excluding the other two. The revision isolates the mechanism better than the first run did, because its post-shutdown phase has no race with the shutdown itself: in the three verify cases (parsed result events at indices 1, 7 and 13) only 4, 3 and 3 of the 8 calls made after Shutdown() had returned were answered, all with 'raft is already shutdown', while the other 4, 5 and 5 returned futures that were still incomplete 500ms later and can never be answered because the run loop, the FSM goroutine and every other reader of verifyCh have already exited. That is 14 of 24 post-shutdown VerifyLeader calls stranded, and it is a per-call coin flip rather than a rare race. The same receipt shows the contrast in the two other call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all 48 of their post-shutdown calls with the shutdown error (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17), and no call in the racing phase of any case was left incomplete (0 stuck out of 128 per case, with 128 answered in the no-shutdown control at index 19). The source explains exactly that split. VerifyLeader builds a verifyFuture whose init() allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), so nothing sets ShutdownCh and deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117); the call then selects between the closed shutdown channel and a send into verifyCh, which is buffered with 64 slots (api.go 576), so the send is ready with no receiver and the select returns an unanswerable future whenever it picks that case. Barrier and ApplyLog use the same select shape (api.go 907-926 and 874-899) but send to applyCh, which is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh is set (api.go 549), so once the loop has exited their send cannot be selected and the shutdown case always wins. The repository's own test file already notes the class as a TODO for Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration (raft_test.go 38-42), which is an admission of the gap rather than a contract that permits it. The first receipt adds the racing form of the same defect: with 64 calls issued just before Shutdown and a 1500ms wait, two of its three verify trials left 9 and 41 futures incomplete while the control left none (indices 1, 7, 13 and 19 there). The revision's racing phase left none, so that form is timing dependent; the post-shutdown form is not, and it is the one the account now rests on.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the revision: 0 of 128 calls per case were left incomplete, so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in either run (0 of 192 and 0 of 192 in the first receipt; 0 of 384 in the revision), which limits the defect to the VerifyLeader path unless BatchApplyCh is enabled.
Every call that was answered in these runs returned success or the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, so the defect is confined to calls whose future is never served.

The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence that the gap was noticed; it does not make the documented ErrRaftShutdown behaviour any less expected for a caller.
limitations: The post-shutdown counts come from 24 VerifyLeader calls in one execution (14 stranded); they bound the mechanism, not a population rate, and the per-call split is consistent with an unbiased select rather than a measured probability.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source (no reader of verifyCh remains and ShutdownCh is nil on these futures) rather than observed indefinitely.
A single-voter node with in-memory transport and 50ms timeouts is used, so no peer round trip or networked shutdown is involved.
A BatchApplyCh configuration, where applyCh becomes buffered and the apply path should inherit the same defect, has not been measured.

interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and three retained runs now answer it for VerifyLeader while showing that the same strand follows channel buffering rather than the API. In this run the VerifyLeader strand reproduced (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13, comparison 4 holds), and so did the contrast: with the default unbuffered applyCh, Barrier and Apply answered every one of their eight post-shutdown calls in all three trials (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17; comparisons 2 and 3 hold). The new batched cases, where BatchApplyCh buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries, show the flip: Barrier answered 4, 5 and 6 of eight post-shutdown calls (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply answered 4, 4 and 3 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 4, 3 and 2 and then 4, 4 and 5 futures unanswered after 500ms, in each case with the rest answered by 'raft is already shutdown'. The mechanism is therefore pinned by a configuration change: only the channel's buffering differs between the answered and the stranded cases, since Config.BatchApplyCh exists exactly to buffer applyCh and its own comment warns that it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply. The declared comparisons for those new cases came back unresolved rather than satisfied, because the batched cases reuse the same trial and kind as the unbuffered ones, so the setup event that admits each result event is ambiguous; the event values themselves are recorded and decisive, and a corrected revision that gives the batched cases distinct trial identifiers and records batch_apply_ch on the setup event as well is submitted with this update. What the three runs together establish is narrower and firmer than the first account: the racing phase is the fragile part (9 and 41 of 64 in the first run, 0 of 128 in the two later ones), while the post-shutdown phase is stable, and the defect is confined to call kinds whose channel is buffered, with VerifyLeader always in that set and the apply path only when BatchApplyCh is enabled.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the two later runs (0 of 128 per case), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.
Without BatchApplyCh, Barrier and Apply never stranded a future in any run (0 of 192, 0 of 384 and 0 of 384 attempts), so the defect does not touch the default apply path.
